newsitem.title: USA: Arkansans celebrate favorite son Clinton's triumph.
newsitem.headline: Arkansans celebrate favorite son Clinton's triumph.

text.p: A festive mood gripped President Bill Clinton's hometown on Tuesday night as his most faithful supporters savored a political victory that made him the first Democrat to win re-election in 52 years.

"No words can convey the gratitude I feel tonight for the honour that has been given to me," an exultant Clinton declared after the outcome was clear. His re-election came just two years after he was blamed for a Democratic debacle in mid-term congressional elections and pronounced politically dead by many experts.

Clinton, flanked by wife Hillary and daughter Chelsea, 16, and Vice President Al Gore and Tipper Gore, celebrated his election victory in a speech at the Old State House -- a large white Greek Revival structure where he first claimed the mantle of leadership in the 1992 election.

Speaking to a huge throng -- and via television to the U.S. public at large -- Clinton remembered people who backed him in good times and bad, and thanked Republicans Bob Dole and Jack Kemp for their public service.
Saluting Dole "for the campaign that he fought so bravely to the very last minute," Clinton said: "On behalf of the American people, I wish him well and Godspeed."

While the voters gave Clinton an electoral landslide, they also kept the Republicans in control of Congress. "America has told every one of us, Democrats and Republicans and independents, loud and clear, it is time to put politics aside, join together and get the job done," he said.

When the race was decided, Clinton was in a staff suite on the 18th floor of the Excelsior Hotel, his election headquarters, and walked around the room embracing staff members, White House spokesman Mike McCurry said. "Obviously, the president is in very good spirits," he told reporters.

Asked if Clinton would meet his vanquished rival in the near future, McCurry said: "You've heard on many occasions the president say how much he respects Senator Dole ... (but) it's premature at this point to talk about how that relationship will develop."
Even before the voting ended, an exuberant crowd had gathered outside Clinton's hotel, turning downtown Little Rock streets into one big party.
For Arkansans, Clinton's duplication of a feat no Democrat had managed since Franklin Roosevelt was re-elected in 1944, represented a vindication of sorts.

They had watched in dismay as the image of their state took a beating from the Whitewater case and other scandals that brought disaster to many native sons who accompanied Clinton to Washington after he wrested the White House from George Bush in 1992.

The list of Arkansas casualties during Clinton's first term was long and grim -- deputy White House counsel Vince Foster, a Clinton friend from kindergarten, killed himself; Assistant Attorney General Webb Hubbell, a onetime law partner of First Lady Hillary Rodham Clinton, went to jail; and several other "Friends of Bill," including former Surgeon General Joycelyn Elders, were sacked.
But those dark memories were all eclipsed by their former governor's big moment. McCurry said Clinton regarded his triumph at the polls as "a somewhat humbling experience."
"He knows he's going to have to work every day" to meet the challenges facing the country as it prepares to enter the 21st century, the spokesman said.

With the election in hand, attention focused on the people who will surround Clinton for the next four years. White House chief of staff Leon Panetta is among those departing -- he wants to go home to California and perhaps run for governor there in 1996.
Former Small Business Administration chief Erskine Bowles leads the list of possible replacements, but is resisting Clinton's entreaties to return to government service, White House sources said.

Secretary of State Warren Christopher, one of many cabinet officers in Little Rock for the victory party, was also expected to step down. Sources said former Senate Democratic leader George Mitchell, U.N. ambassador Madeleine Albright and former assistant Secretary of State Richard Holbrooke, who brokered the Bosnia peace agreement, were on the short list of contenders for Christopher's job.
